We will tell you what is known, who says what, and what is still not known. Some chapters describe killings and sexual violence. We tell them plainly and without detail.

Somalia 1988. In May 1988, rebels of the Somali National Movement attacked Boor-oh and then Har-gaysa, in northern Somalia. The army answered with artillery, air raids and mass executions. The violence fell overwhelmingly on civilians of the Ee-sahk clan-family, in what is today Somaliland. An investigator for the United States State Department, Robert Gersony, gave a deliberately cautious minimum estimate. He estimated that at least five thousand unarmed Ee-sahk civilians were purposefully murdered by the army between May 1988 and March 1989. In January 1990, the human-rights group Africa Watch estimated fifty to sixty thousand war-related deaths since May 1988, including deaths from attacks, wounds and disease. By Africa Watch's estimate of January 1990, nearly half a million people had fled abroad, most of them to Ethiopia. The same investigators also recorded killings by the rebels, of non-Ee-sahk civilians and of refugees from Ethiopia, on a much smaller scale. Many researchers, and Somaliland's government, call the campaign against the Ee-sahk a genocide. The court cases discussed here did not decide that question.

The land and its peoples. Somalia lies in the Horn of Africa. Its north-west borders Djibouti and Ethiopia. Many Somalis share a language and a religion. But Somalia also has minority communities, with their own histories and identities. Somali society is organised into clans. The Ee-sahk are commonly described as a clan-family: a large community of related clans, with descent generally traced through the father's line. The Ee-sahk formed much of the population of Har-gaysa, Boor-oh and the land around them. Other northern areas were home to other communities, among them the Gada-boorsee, the Issa, the Dhool-ba-hanteh and the War-san-gelly. The main northern towns were Har-gaysa and Boor-oh. Berbera was the north's port. Somaliland claims the territory of the former British protectorate in the north.

Barre's Somalia. Mo-hammed See-yaad Barreh took power in a military coup on the twenty-first of October 1969. His government said it stood against clannism, the politics of clan loyalty. The historian Markus Hoehne and others describe how Barre came to rely more and more on selected relatives, officers and allies, including people from the Mareh-haan, Oga-den and Dhool-ba-hanteh clans. Not every member of those clans supported him. In March 1978 Somalia was defeated in the Oga-den war against Ethiopia. Hundreds of thousands of refugees from the Oga-den, in Ethiopia, then crossed into Somalia. Many were settled in camps near the north-western towns. Africa Watch reports that the government formed armed groups among these refugees and conscripted many into the army. These refugees appear twice in this story. The government recruited and armed some of them. Rebel attacks on the camps also killed unarmed refugees.

The Somali National Movement. The Somali National Movement was founded in London on the sixth of April 1981, by Ee-sahk emigrants. From here on we call it the S N M. In 1982 the S N M moved its bases to Ethiopia, across the border from the north-west. The S N M drew its fighters mainly from the Ee-sahk. But being Ee-sahk did not make a person a rebel. Most of the people in this story were civilians who had no part in the fighting. In 1988 the S N M's chairman was Ahmed Mo-hammed Mohamoud, known as See-laanyo.

Why the title says genocide. The title of this page uses a name that many researchers and Somaliland's government use: the Ee-sahk genocide. Genocide is a crime in international law. It means acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part. Researchers and Somaliland's government use this description. A later study commissioned by United Nations offices is reported to have concluded that genocide occurred. That study was not a court judgment. The United Nations human-rights reports cited here described mass killings as war crimes and crimes against humanity. That wording does not settle whether genocide also occurred. The court cases discussed here did not decide whether these events were genocide. We explain this in chapter twenty-nine.

The investigators. Robert Gersony wrote his report for the United States State Department in August 1989. It rests on three hundred and two interviews, two hundred and fifty-two of them about the north, gathered in Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya between March and May 1989. Gersony spoke with Ee-sahk refugees, with non-Ee-sahk Somalis who stayed, and with refugees from Ethiopia in the camps. Africa Watch, a human-rights organisation, published its report in January 1990. Its researchers interviewed newly arrived refugees in Djibouti and in Britain in 1989. The government did not allow Africa Watch into the north. The two reports used different witnesses. Both documented major army abuses in the same northern towns, although their evidence and some of their conclusions differ. Later evidence came from United Nations experts, forensic scientists who examined graves, and two civil cases in American courts.

How this page tells it. Each line carries a tag. "Established" means the evidence strongly supports it. "Government" marks a government account, with the government named. "S N M" marks a statement by the S N M itself. "Scholarship", "press" and "advocacy" mark a scholar's view, a newspaper or a campaigning group. "Witness" marks one person's testimony. "Estimate" marks an uncertain number. "Disputed" means sources disagree, or rest on one unconfirmed account. "Court" marks a court record, and says what kind. "Report" marks a human-rights or official investigation, and names it. Numbers may differ because sources count different deaths, places or periods, and use different methods. We give each number with who counted it, and what it counts. We never add them together.

Refugees and militias. After 1978, Africa Watch reports, the government encouraged armed groups among the refugees from Ethiopia. It also records abuses along the border by the Western Somali Liberation Front. Africa Watch says that militias encouraged by the government "committed atrocities against the Ee-sahk civilian population living along the Somali/Ethiopian border". On the thirtieth of March 1982, twenty-one Ee-sahk elders sent a memorandum to President Barre. They complained that the Western Somali Liberation Front subjected rural people to "murder and robbery". They complained that northerners were shut out of running the refugee programme. And they said the north was neglected in trade, industry and public works. In 1980 a new military commander was appointed in the north, Major General Mo-hammed Hashi Gani. Africa Watch says the military commanders were also, in effect, the governors.

The Har-gaysa Group. In December 1981 the authorities arrested about thirty doctors, engineers and teachers in Har-gaysa. They had organised volunteer work to improve the city's hospital. Africa Watch calls them the Har-gaysa Group. Africa Watch treats their arrest as the political trigger in the north. Their trial in February 1982 set off demonstrations in Har-gaysa and across the north. Witnesses date the serious disturbances to about the twentieth of February. A curfew was imposed. In Somaliland the group is remembered as "Ooffo", and the protests as "Dhagah Toor". In the same month the government tightened its control over payments for imports, and confiscated goods at Berbera port.

Courts of the emergency. From 1982, emergency regulations put civilians in the north under military courts. The Mobile Military Court travelled from town to town. Africa Watch describes a court system in which defendants had little protection. In Har-gaysa, its executions took place at Badhka, an open ground in the south-west of the city. Alongside the court were a Regional Security Council, chaired by the military commander, and the military intelligence force. Africa Watch describes the three as one system of control. The court's prosecutor was a colonel, Yusuf Muse, known as Yusuf Dheh-reh. Africa Watch says he regularly demanded the death sentence. For a time, from 1986, he was replaced by Colonel Abdillahi Debob. Africa Watch says Debob "refused to carry out some unlawful executions".

Reprisals, 1984. Africa Watch dates the start of systematic reprisal killings to 1984, when the S N M stepped up its raids from Ethiopia. On the fifteenth of October 1984, six men were shot at Gogol Wa-naag, near Arab-see-yo. On the seventeenth of November, twenty-six Ee-sahk men were executed in Har-gaysa after sentences by the Mobile Military Court. Africa Watch says nine were civilians and seventeen were S N M fighters. The town's elders were forced to watch. In December, forty-three men were executed in Boor-oh. Witnesses told Africa Watch that the charges against them had been changed from ordinary crimes to links with the S N M. From 1984, Africa Watch also documents the destruction of water reservoirs, the killing and seizing of livestock, and the laying of mines on roads and near reservoirs. Water and herds were what rural families lived on.

General Morgan's report. At the end of 1986, General Mo-hammed Said Hersi, known as Morgan, took over as military commander in the north. Africa Watch says he brought in photo identity cards to control people's movements. In February 1987, a confidential report from General Morgan to President Barre leaked to the international press. Africa Watch writes that the report set out policies Morgan had been carrying out to "liquidate" what he called the "Ee-sahk problem". Africa Watch lists the measures. Confiscating Ee-sahk property. Suspending business licences and freezing bank accounts. Removing Ee-sahk from sensitive government posts. Relocating villages. Destroying water reservoirs. And resettling refugees from Ethiopia on Ee-sahk land. Africa Watch attributed the report to Morgan. The copy shown on this page is a later reproduction, which we have not independently authenticated, and we have not found his response to this document. Later reproductions often call it the "Letter of Death". In January 1987, S N M fighters kidnapped a medical team of the French charity Médecins Sans Frontières, Doctors Without Borders. The team was released after about a week. In May 1987, the French news agency reported that an army raid at Bihin refugee camp, near Berbera, forced two to three hundred refugees into the army.

The door closes. At the end of 1987, Africa Watch says, Yusuf Dheh-reh returned as prosecutor of the military court, and mass executions began again. In March 1988 President Barre visited the north. At a rally in Har-gaysa's stadium, students threw stones. Witnesses say the presidential guard fired into the crowd and killed five students. During the same visit, on the fourteenth of March, twenty-four or twenty-five Ee-sahk men were executed at Gabbi-lay and Tog Wa-jaaleh, near the Ethiopian border. Witnesses described it as a reprisal for an S N M attack. On the third of April 1988, Somalia and Ethiopia signed a peace accord. Each promised not to help the other's rebels. The S N M's bases in Ethiopia were now at risk. Less than two months later, it attacked.

Friday in Boor-oh. On Friday the twenty-seventh of May 1988, S N M fighters attacked Boor-oh. Africa Watch says they "captured the town in about two hours". They took the military compound at the airport, the Goan Ad compound outside the town, the police stations and the prison. Crowds of townspeople followed the fighters. The S N M questioned residents about local officials. Several officials named as abusive were shot, among them the local military commander, the head of the secret service and the police commander. A Boor-oh resident, Ahmed Saeed Elmi, told Africa Watch that the fighters spared soldiers known to be fair to civilians, and killed men whom residents accused of abuses. Those accusations did not justify executing prisoners. Africa Watch condemns these killings. Under the laws of war, people in custody, or no longer able to fight, must not be executed. How long the S N M held the town is unclear. One passage in Africa Watch says the fighters withdrew to their base by five in the afternoon. Other accounts describe the S N M in the town for days. The same day, the army arrested Ee-sahk men in Berbera, Shaykh, Erri-gahvo and Bo-rahma, towns the S N M had not attacked.

The army's answer in Boor-oh. Witnesses say soldiers went on a rampage in Boor-oh on the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth of May, looting and killing. Witnesses also say the army used loudspeakers to call non-Ee-sahk residents to leave, and gave them transport out. After that evacuation, the shelling began. Aircraft began bombing the town on Tuesday the thirty-first of May. An American government investigating office, the General Accounting Office, reported in May 1989 that the army "responded to the S N M attacks in May 1988 with extreme force". It said the army used "artillery and aerial shelling in heavily populated urban centers", and tanks in Boor-oh. Gersony judged that civilian deaths in the crossfire, in Har-gaysa and Boor-oh, may have reached the thousands. The government denied that civilians had been killed, or civilian targets deliberately destroyed. It blamed "bandits", and called civilian casualties "exceptional episodes".

The S N M's prisoners in Boor-oh. Within days of the attack, Gersony found, the S N M rounded up several hundred men in Boor-oh, most of them non-Ee-sahk. About fifty were executed after hasty military trials. A witness said one trial lasted ten minutes. Some of the dead may have been soldiers or officers. Others were civilians who had played no part in government or the army. Gersony concluded that S N M commanders "must have been aware of and at least condoned these executions". He also disclosed a limit. His five witnesses to these events, a Ha-wee-yeh, an Oga-deni, two Dhool-ba-hanteh and a War-san-gelly, were found for him by the government. Africa Watch records that the S N M took some arrested non-Ee-sahk civilians toward their home villages. On the way, Ee-sahk nomads who had armed themselves for the S N M stopped one convoy and shot its Da-rood passengers. These accounts do not identify which S N M commanders were responsible for the executions.

Arrests before the attack. In Har-gaysa, the arrests began as soon as the news from Boor-oh arrived. Jama Osman Samater had been a political prisoner from 1982 until February 1988. He told Africa Watch he was leaving Friday prayers when he heard of the attack on Boor-oh, and that a curfew whistle blew that afternoon. The next morning, the twenty-eighth of May, he saw soldiers herding people into cars. Africa Watch reports that fifty-three businessmen and elders were seized that day. Fearing re-arrest, he shaved his head, dressed as a nomad and hid with neighbours. He said soldiers searched his house that night and took its valuables. Detainees were held at the army's sector headquarters at Birjeh, at the Malka Door-dooro military compound, at the central prison and at sites of the National Security Service, the country's main secret service. Some were taken to Mandera prison, between Har-gaysa and Berbera. On the first of June, witnesses say, the S N M freed the sixty detainees held there.

The night attack. The S N M attacked Har-gaysa on the thirty-first of May 1988. Both reports give this date, and Africa Watch gives the time as a quarter past two in the morning. Khadra Mu-hoomed Abdi, also a former political prisoner, was hiding in her aunt's house in the Doom-boo-look district. She told Africa Watch that next morning she saw her own district, near the Radio Station, burning. She said government loudspeakers claimed that a small rebel force had been driven out, and urged residents to return home. She said people who believed the announcement were killed. Gersony found that the S N M spread its fighters, in uniform and in ordinary clothes, through the crowded, mainly Ee-sahk neighbourhoods. He wrote that this put civilians "in the immediate line of fire". Gersony did not use this to clear either side. He wrote that neither side was absolved of responsibility for avoidable harm to Har-gaysa's civilians. The S N M's defensive line ran behind the Radio Station. The government kept the airport and the Sha'ab district.

Shelling and bombing. For a day or two, Africa Watch says, the army held back. Then it counter-attacked with heavy weapons. Long-range guns on the hilltops near the zoo, and on the hills behind Badhka, shelled the city. Aircraft took off from Har-gaysa's own airport to bomb the city. Witnesses say pilots flew low over the people trying to escape. Gersony recorded that the armed forces "used military aircraft to strafe and bomb residential areas in which S N M forces were dispersed". Hassan Ismail told Africa Watch of his disbelief that aircraft were taking off from Har-gaysa's own airport to bomb the city. Jama Osman Samater described the shelling as relentless. He said he lost any sense of fear, and that in prison only he had suffered, while here everyone was a victim. Doom-boo-look, south of the dry river bed that divides the city, suffered most. Africa Watch says the S N M had not entered it. A French hospital technician, Jean Metenier, told reporters after his evacuation that at least two dozen people had been shot against the wall of his house. One witness quoted by Africa Watch named the aircraft as British-made Hunters and MiG jets, with small Italian planes spotting targets. This identification comes from that one witness. Later press accounts describe an air force pilot who refused to bomb the city and flew his jet to Djibouti instead.

Executions in the city. Witnesses told Africa Watch of men shot in lines into a trench inside the Malka Door-dooro military compound. A prison employee said seventy Ee-sahk soldiers held as detainees were shot there on the fourth day of the arrests. A detained truck driver described executions of at least thirty people a day, from about the seventh to the fifteenth of June, at Qaybta, the regional commander's headquarters. He said that on one day, eighty Ee-sahk soldiers, from Gabbi-lay, Darar Weyne and Bogol Jirreh, were shot along the dry river bed. Witnesses described soldiers searching house to house and killing the men they found. One father, they said, lost seven sons. The investigations also documented torture and severe mistreatment of people in detention. Africa Watch reports that the army armed non-Ee-sahk civilians. It released non-Ee-sahk prisoners, including men convicted of murder, to guard Ee-sahk detainees or to fight. Across the wider region, in the accounts he collected, Gersony recorded two hundred and thirty-three civilian deaths in thirty-two incidents of summary executions and other killings. They spanned several places and years, from 1982 to 1989; about two thirds fell between late May and August 1988.

A city in ruins. Several Africa Watch witnesses place the S N M's withdrawal from Har-gaysa in August 1988. They say the army kept shelling afterwards, looted, and laid mines in buildings, among them the Union Hotel. The sources differ on when the army regained control. The American General Accounting Office gives the thirtieth of May for Boor-oh and the thirteenth of July for Har-gaysa. Its report also refers to military control of Har-gaysa from late July, while Africa Watch witnesses place the S N M's withdrawal from Har-gaysa in August. Gersony found that seventy per cent of the army killings his witnesses described happened between the twenty-seventh of May and the thirty-first of August 1988. The American embassy estimated that seventy per cent of Har-gaysa was damaged or destroyed. The General Accounting Office said its own rough inspection confirmed this. The State Department's human-rights report for 1989 measured something narrower. It said about ninety per cent of the Ee-sahk homes, businesses and property in Har-gaysa were destroyed or severely damaged.

Berbera: the roundups. Berbera, the northern port, was not attacked by the S N M during the 1988 offensive, and remained in government hands. Gersony found that from shortly after the twenty-seventh of May until at least September, soldiers "systematically collected large numbers of Ee-sahk males on the sole basis of their clan association". They were held near Berbera airport. At night they were taken out in groups, killed, and buried in mass graves. Gersony's witnesses described groups of five to fifty. They placed one burial site about a kilometre from the end of the runway. Africa Watch, from other witnesses, describes batches of thirty to forty, at a site about ten kilometres from the town, near the airport, mainly in June. Gersony's count is "at least five hundred, and perhaps many more" Ee-sahk men, killed "apparently solely because they were Ee-sahks". Africa Watch, separately, also says at least five hundred. Most victims, Africa Watch says, were seasonal workers from Har-gaysa and Boor-oh, hired to load livestock and unload goods at the port. Among the dead whose names it learned were a restaurant owner, a taxi driver, a cement-factory worker, a port employee and a soldier. A witness, Kaiser Ismail Adan, told Africa Watch that the town learned of the killings from a survivor, Abdee Waal, who escaped from the first group. The witness said soldiers later took Abdee Waal from the hospital; what became of him was not known to that witness.

Berbera: the ship and the prison. On the twenty-first of June 1988, a ship, the Emviyara, docked at Berbera with people deported from Saudi Arabia. Witnesses say military intelligence officers separated out twenty-nine Ee-sahk passengers. Eight of them were later killed. Africa Watch records a witness account of eleven men killed east of Batalale, near Berbera. A prison in Berbera built for a hundred and twenty people held four hundred and eighty-five at one point. A detainee accused Berbera's military commander, General Ahmed Warsame, of responsibility for killings. This is an allegation recorded by Africa Watch, not a court's finding. The same detainee described his replacement, around July, General Yusuf Talan, more favourably, and said he released forty sick and elderly detainees. The sources reviewed here do not establish any judicial finding about either officer.

Towns not attacked in the May offensive. Africa Watch describes a similar pattern in smaller towns not attacked by the S N M during the May 1988 offensive. In Shaykh, armed refugees from the Bihin and Bee-yolay camps did most of the killing and looting, witnesses said. In Erri-gahvo, non-Ee-sahk men were armed and Ee-sahk men detained. In Arab-see-yo, witnesses described looting, and elderly people shot, in early June. In Bo-rahma, Ee-sahk drivers were arrested on the twenty-ninth of May. Far to the south, in the capital Mogadishu, more than three hundred Ee-sahk were detained. Africa Watch's framing is "a government at war with its own people". It says the army came to treat being Ee-sahk as being "anti-government". Gersony wrote that in the killings he recorded, "the appearance that victims were selected for these killings principally because of their ethnic identity is unmistakable".

On the roads. When the fighting in the towns grew worse, people fled on foot and in vehicles, carrying the old and the sick in hand carts. The General Accounting Office found that the evacuation of Har-gaysa and Boor-oh began in early June. Refugees told it they were strafed by aircraft while gathering their families on the edges of the cities. Mo-hammed Karshe Mo-hammed, a former seaman, told Africa Watch that after nine days of fighting his family left with nothing. "Because of the planes you never lost the fear," he said, "so you just kept going." Another man, Yusuf, told Africa Watch that people felt unsafe whether they stayed or fled. Witnesses describe bombing from six in the morning to six in the evening at places where people had gathered: Biyaha Shinaha, Annayo, Udaan and Geed-Debleh, where there was a centre for the wounded. A woman Africa Watch calls Fadumo, not her real name, set out with about a hundred people for Annayo, west of Har-gaysa. She said they learned that a bomber always came after a spotter plane, and hid in the bush when the spotter appeared. Africa Watch says the planes "followed some people into Ethiopia". Gersony judged that ground and air attacks on people fleeing "probably resulted in the deaths of hundreds of asylum seekers". Most refugees reached Ethiopia between June and September 1988.

The camps in Ethiopia. Across the border, the largest camps were Harti-shake and Harti-shake B. Smaller camps were set up at Camp Aboker, Rabasso and Daror. Jama Osman Samater told Africa Watch that at Harti-shake there were no tents in the first week, and no water. His family drank muddy rainwater from puddles and ate raw corn until they got ration cards. Yassin Karshe Mo-hammed, who stayed in the camps from August 1988 to February 1989, described severe shortages of food and water, and many deaths among small children. Africa Watch reports malaria, jaundice, meningitis and diarrhoea in the camps. Gersony's report gave an estimated three hundred thousand to five hundred thousand arrivals in eastern Ethiopia between May 1988 and January 1989, up to four thousand a day. Africa Watch, in January 1990, counted over four hundred thousand in Ethiopia, about forty thousand in Djibouti, and close to four hundred thousand displaced inside Somalia. The State Department counted three hundred and twenty-four thousand refugees in Ethiopia and thirty thousand in Djibouti at the end of 1989. These are separate estimates, from different dates and sources. They are not directly comparable. The United Nations refugee agency later said Harti-shake held more than two hundred and fifty thousand people at its peak.

Refugees as soldiers. Gersony found that for many years before May 1988, the army forcibly conscripted refugees from the United Nations camps, despite strong protests from the United Nations refugee agency. After the twenty-seventh of May, he found, "at least several hundred and perhaps more" camp refugees "were provided weapons and induced by the Somali Armed Forces to become active in para-military operations". Witnesses saw armed refugees in uniform helping to round up Ee-sahk men in Berbera. The refugees told Gersony they had asked for weapons to defend themselves, after repeated S N M attacks on their camps. Africa Watch stressed that recruitment and arming also came before these attacks. It cited press reports of the 1987 conscription raid at Bihin, and of refugee-agency protests in January 1988 over the conscription of up to seven thousand refugees. Gersony, for his part, documented the earlier forced conscription separately, while recording the refugees' accounts of being armed later for self-defence. The General Accounting Office reported that in July 1988 the United Nations refugee agency and other observers had noticed armed refugees in six of fourteen camps. The government told the refugee agency they were armed "for their own protection". An American arms shipment arrived at Berbera on the twenty-eighth of June 1988. The General Accounting Office confirmed its use in the northern conflict. Africa Watch reported that American rifles were used to arm refugees. Gersony also recorded a Gada-boorsee clan militia, the "Gadabursi Front", which was not part of the government but had at times received army weapons.

Attacks on the camps. From about the thirtieth of May 1988 and through the rest of that year, Gersony found, the S N M carried out dozens of attacks on United Nations camps for refugees from Ethiopia. The first attack, on the thirtieth or thirty-first of May, struck the Agga-bar and Laas Dhooreh camps, north-west of Har-gaysa. Forty-three people were killed. Gersony reported that neither camp had been armed before those attacks. He wrote that the aim "appeared to be to employ violence to force the refugees out of the area". Refugees in the camps described two hundred and forty-one deaths across nine camps to Gersony. The highest tolls were at Dam, Adiades, Sa-baad, Bee-yolay and Bixin. About six in ten of those killed were men, including elderly men. About four in ten were women and children. Gersony "conservatively estimated" that at least four hundred unarmed refugees were killed in these attacks. The refugees said about ninety per cent of their dead were killed before the camps received weapons. Africa Watch accepted that S N M attacks had killed hundreds of refugees, and condemned those killings. It also reported that the S N M diverted relief supplies meant for refugees. The General Accounting Office reported that, during its visit in early March 1989, an S N M attack on a truck killed eleven refugees. Its investigators were told this reflected a pattern of attacks intended to force refugees from the area. Gersony's overall finding was that both sides gravely violated the protection that refugees in United Nations camps were owed.

The S N M's other abuses. Gersony found that in the first three months of the offensive, S N M fighters killed unarmed civilians in incidents that together may have caused at least several hundred deaths. The victims, he wrote, included people fleeing who resisted looting, and "men sought out and killed apparently only because they were not Ee-sahks". In one region, prisoners of war were reported executed after questioning. His interview accounts recorded seventy-six such deaths outside the camps: five at checkpoints, twenty-one near battle areas and fifty in Boor-oh. This was not a complete count. Africa Watch says that once the government began arming non-Ee-sahk civilians, young men who had newly joined the S N M killed some unarmed non-Ee-sahk civilians. Refugees remembered Hassan Abole, a teacher at Har-gaysa Technical Institute, and a teacher of Koranic studies, both shot while fleeing. Africa Watch found no evidence that the S N M "as an organization had a policy of deliberately targeting civilians" because they were not Ee-sahk. Ee-sahk refugees told Africa Watch they were angry at the S N M's stern warnings not to take revenge on civilians. But the S N M treated armed non-Ee-sahk civilians as part of the government's forces. The S N M also shot Ee-sahk it suspected of spying for the government: two nomads near Geed-Debleh in 1987, businessmen in Har-gaysa, and in November 1988, at Ha-baas Wayneh, Ee-sahk women married to soldiers. The State Department's report for 1989 said S N M fighters around Erri-gahvo in March 1989 "killed a number of unresisting civilians". It judged that the S N M committed abuses "to a lesser extent" than the government.

The other northern clans. The historian Markus Hoehne describes support for Barre among leaders and armed groups from several non-Ee-sahk northern communities, among them the Gada-boorsee, the Dhool-ba-hanteh, the War-san-gelly and the Issa. These communities were not politically uniform. He gives different reasons for different groups. Some had kinship ties to the regime. Others feared domination by the S N M. Some were armed by the state. A witness told Africa Watch that the government spread claims that the S N M threatened the survival of Da-rood communities. When the war broke out, the government gave transport to non-Ee-sahk residents. But it could not move everyone. Africa Watch says thousands of non-Ee-sahk fled the bombing and shelling alongside the Ee-sahk. Gersony noted that once the non-Ee-sahk had left the big towns, the main concentrations of non-Ee-sahk people in the region were the refugee camps. He also recorded acts of courage. Witnesses told him of non-Ee-sahk civilians who saved the lives of Ee-sahk civilians, and of Ee-sahk civilians who saved the lives of non-Ee-sahk.

War in the countryside. After the summer of 1988, the war became a rural insurgency, a war of raids in the countryside. From June to September 1988, the army and armed refugees raided villages between Har-gaysa and Berbera. In July and November 1988, villages in the eastern regions were attacked, around El Af-wayn and Kal-shaykh. Witnesses say troops based at the El Af-wayn secondary school killed about fifty people in the first attack. An Australian aid agency, Community Aid Abroad, reported that after a mine killed two soldiers in El Af-wayn district, the military commander of Sa-nahg ordered two hundred nomads killed. It said a hundred and three were killed the next day. Both reports document sexual violence against Ee-sahk women by soldiers. Africa Watch says mines were laid widely, on roads, at reservoirs and around army camps. It adds that it could not investigate the mines itself. Human Rights Watch's report for 1989 adds "the poisoning of wells" to the means used against the population. Where it lacked troops, the army relied on armed refugees and clan militias.

Erri-gahvo and Sa-nahg. In Erri-gahvo, in the region of Sa-nahg, Ee-sahk men were detained from late May 1988, and non-Ee-sahk men were armed. On the twelfth of January 1989, Community Aid Abroad withdrew from Sa-nahg. Its statement said the military occupation of Erri-gahvo had driven most of the town's people into the bush, and described a "scorched earth" policy in the villages of the El Af-wayn plains. Its spokesman, Peter Kieseker, said of the government's policies there: "Genocide is the only word for it." A British newspaper, the Independent, quoted him on the thirteenth of February 1989. In March 1989, the S N M briefly entered Erri-gahvo. A Canadian government compilation gives a three-hour occupation on the sixteenth of March; an Africa Watch witness says the end of March. Clan militias then carried out reprisals against Ee-sahk civilians. The State Department reported that S N M fighters around Erri-gahvo that month killed unresisting civilians.

The world takes notice. In August 1988, a State Department mission led by Kenneth Bleakley confirmed reports of the bombing. Africa Watch's account of September 1990 says a "Reconciliation Committee" set up in January 1989 visited only Berbera and Boor-oh, and had not published findings. In January 1989, Prime Minister Mo-hammed Ali Sama-tar offered an amnesty in London. On the twelfth of March 1989, a hundred and twenty-five Ee-sahk detainees were released from Laanta Boor prison, near Mogadishu. The government refused Africa Watch access to the north, despite a promise from the Prime Minister. Gersony's report was dated August 1989, and became public later that year. The killings did not stop. Africa Watch recorded forty-seven Ee-sahk men shot at Jezira Beach, near Mogadishu, on the sixteenth of July 1989. It recorded twelve young men executed at Hahi, near Ood-wayneh, on Christmas Day 1989, and seventeen Ee-sahk men shot in central Berbera on the sixteenth of August 1990.

The north is taken. By October 1990, the S N M controlled almost all of the north-west outside the besieged army garrisons. At the end of January 1991, it captured the garrisons of Har-gaysa, Berbera and Boor-oh. The day each town fell is not recorded in our sources. At the same time, on the twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh of January, See-yaad Barreh fled Mogadishu. His government had fallen. The S N M then advanced into Gada-boorsee areas, taking Deela and Bo-rahma in early 1991. A Canadian refugee-board compilation, citing contemporary news and aid reports, describes S N M violence in the Bo-rahma area as "ethnic cleansing", and reports Deela's partial destruction. It is a compilation, not an investigation or a court's finding. Gada-boorsee communities remember killings and displacement in this advance. The sources reviewed here do not establish the death toll. Accounts also describe fighting with local militias at Deela. Fighting does not excuse attacks on civilians. In February 1991, clan delegates met at Berbera: Issa, Gada-boorsee, Dhool-ba-hanteh, War-san-gelly and Ee-sahk. A larger conference of the northern clans opened at Boor-oh on the twenty-seventh of April. On the eighteenth of May 1991, the S N M leadership and delegates at the Boor-oh conference declared Somaliland an independent republic, within the borders of the former British protectorate. Support for separation was not unanimous. The S N M chairman, Abdirahman Ahmed Ali Tuur, announced it. Peace was not complete. There was fighting in 1992, and again from 1994 to 1996. Separation remained contested, including among Dhool-ba-hanteh leaders and communities. In 1993, a conference at Bo-rahma chose Mo-hammed Haji Ibrahim Ee-gaal as president, with a Gada-boorsee vice-president, Abdirahman Aw Ali Farah, in a power-sharing settlement.

Graves and investigators. In May 1997, rain uncovered a grave in Har-gaysa. The United Nations' independent expert on human rights in Somalia reported that it held at least two hundred and fifty bodies. That year a committee to investigate war crimes was set up in Har-gaysa. A later United Nations report described its very limited funding. From the seventeenth to the twenty-first of December 1997, forensic scientists from Physicians for Human Rights visited Har-gaysa for the United Nations. They observed ninety-two to a hundred and sixteen alleged graves at three sites: the Milk Factory, Malko Durduro Elementary School and Badhka. They opened two graves for a preliminary examination. These held at least six people. The team concluded that "human rights violations were committed against these individuals". The findings supported the witnesses' accounts of unlawful killings. Later teams, among them Peruvian forensic scientists from 2012, continued exhumations. Many suspected graves remain unexamined, and these investigations do not establish a total death toll. In 2001, the United Nations' independent expert asked General Morgan about responsibility for deaths in Har-gaysa. The expert recorded that he said people had a right to defend their country against perceived foreign intervention. He also "alleged that no civilians had been killed", and that specific graves could not be linked to specific battles. The United Nations expert rejected, as lacking credibility, a claim that the dead in Har-gaysa were refugees killed by the S N M. The sources reviewed here record no trial of General Morgan.

Is it genocide?. Genocide means certain acts committed with the intention of destroying a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, entirely or in substantial part. It is defined in the United Nations convention of 1948. It is the intention to destroy the group that distinguishes this crime. Researchers who describe the campaign against the Ee-sahk as genocide point to the deliberate targeting of civilians because of who they were. A court considering such a claim would need to examine both that intention and whether the convention protects the targeted group. The cases discussed on this page did not determine that question. In 1989, Gersony wrote that victims were selected "principally because of their ethnic identity", and that the Berbera men died "solely because they were Ee-sahks". He did not use the word genocide. In its 1990 report, Africa Watch used the word only once, when quoting the aid worker Peter Kieseker. Its own words were "a government at war with its own people". The United Nations' independent expert, in reports of 1998 and 1999, described the mass killings in terms of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Those descriptions do not exclude genocide: more than one legal category can apply. A United Nations report confirms that United Nations offices commissioned a preliminary study, completed in March 2002 by a consultant, Chris Mburu. Later accounts say it concluded that genocide had occurred. It was a consultant's conclusion, not a court judgment or an official determination by a United Nations body. Scholars have since written about the Ee-sahk case as genocide, among them Mo-hammed Haji Ingi-rees in 2016. Yale University's Genocide Studies Program lists it as a case. The Lemkin Institute, an organisation that campaigns against genocide, called it genocide in 2022. Somaliland's government recognises the events as genocide. Neither of the two American civil cases, in the next chapter, included a genocide claim. They were about torture, killings and detention. The absence of a judgment does not establish that genocide did not occur.

In American courts. Two civil cases were brought in the United States by survivors. Civil cases seek damages for harm. They are not criminal trials. The first was against Mo-hammed Ali Sama-tar, also written Samantar. He was defence minister from 1980 to December 1986, and prime minister from January 1987 to September 1990. The case raised questions of immunity first. In this case, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled in 2012, rejecting Sama-tar's claim to immunity for the alleged violations of fundamental prohibitions of international law. It listed the acts in the case as "torture, summary execution and prolonged arbitrary imprisonment". On the twenty-third of February 2012, Sama-tar accepted a default judgment on civil liability, while denying guilt. The judge then heard evidence on damages. Because he did not contest the case, the court accepted the plaintiffs' facts as true. On that record, Judge Leonie Brinkema found in August 2012 that he had ordered and permitted the abuses, and awarded twenty-one million dollars. The claims were killing, attempted killing, torture, cruel treatment, arbitrary detention, crimes against humanity and war crimes. No claim of genocide was made, and the word does not appear in the judge's opinion. Sama-tar died in 2016, aged eighty-five. The second case was brought by Farhan War-faa against Colonel Yusuf Abdi Ali, known as Tukeh. From May 1987 to July 1988 he commanded an army unit based at Gabbi-lay. On the twenty-first of May 2019, a jury found the colonel liable for torturing Farhan War-faa, and awarded five hundred thousand dollars. It found him not liable for an attempted unlawful killing. Ali denied responsibility. Other claims in that case, including war crimes and crimes against humanity, had been dismissed earlier because they lacked the connection to the United States that the law required. That dismissal did not decide whether those abuses happened. No genocide claim was made. These proceedings established civil liability, not criminal convictions.

In 1988, after S N M attacks on Boor-oh and Har-gaysa, the army shelled and bombed both cities, killed civilians in towns that saw no fighting, and attacked people as they fled. Gersony, for the State Department, and Africa Watch, using different witnesses, both documented major army abuses in the same northern towns. The victims were overwhelmingly Ee-sahk civilians. Gersony found they were chosen "principally because of their ethnic identity". The S N M also killed unarmed non-Ee-sahk civilians, prisoners and refugees from Ethiopia, on a much smaller scale. Africa Watch found no S N M policy of targeting civilians for their clan. Gersony found that S N M commanders must at least have condoned the Boor-oh executions. Refugees from Ethiopia were both forced into the government's service and killed in the S N M's attacks on their camps. At least five thousand unarmed Ee-sahk civilians purposefully murdered by the army, May 1988 to March 1989, not counting crossfire and bombing of battle zones: Gersony's cautious minimum estimate. At least five hundred Ee-sahk men killed in Berbera, perhaps many more: Gersony, and separately Africa Watch. Civilian deaths in the crossfire in Har-gaysa and Boor-oh "may have ascended into the thousands": Gersony. Fifty to sixty thousand killed by government forces, or dead from bombing, shelling, wounds and disease, from May 1988 to January 1990: Africa Watch's estimate of war-related deaths. It did not explain a calculation method in the passages cited here. Killed by the S N M: at least several hundred civilians in the first three months, and at least four hundred refugees in the camp attacks: Gersony. Displaced: nearly half a million abroad and close to four hundred thousand inside Somalia, by Africa Watch's count of January 1990. These figures count different things, over different periods. Some are subsets of others, and some may overlap. They cannot be added together. Later estimates are higher and more uncertain. The court cases discussed here did not decide whether genocide occurred. Sama-tar accepted a default judgment on civil liability, and a court accepted the plaintiffs' facts on that default. The judgment was for torture, killings, detention, crimes against humanity and war crimes. A jury found Colonel Yusuf Abdi Ali liable for the torture of one man, and not liable for an attempted unlawful killing. These proceedings established civil liability, not criminal convictions. An aid-agency spokesman publicly used the word genocide in February 1989. In 2002, a consultant's study commissioned by United Nations offices is reported to have concluded that it was genocide. That is not a judgment or a United Nations determination. The United Nations human-rights reports cited here described the killings as war crimes and crimes against humanity, which does not exclude genocide. Researchers, a campaigning institute and Somaliland's government call it genocide today. Refugees began going home from Harti-shake in 1997, the United Nations refugee agency reports. By the time the camp closed in 2004, the United Nations refugee agency counted two hundred and thirty thousand people returned. Mines remained a danger. By its 2012 account, the mine-clearing organisation the HALO Trust had cleared about eighteen thousand hectares since 1999, and destroyed about a hundred thousand mines and other explosive items. In Har-gaysa, a Somali air force jet stands on a monument in Freedom Square, in memory of the bombing. The thirty-first of May is remembered there. Some Dhool-ba-hanteh writers say Somaliland's national memory centres on the Ee-sahk and on the S N M, and leaves out their own losses. Gada-boorsee communities remember Bo-rahma and Deela in 1991. Somaliland declared independence in 1991. Israel recognised Somaliland as an independent state on the twenty-sixth of December 2025. Recognition of Somaliland as a state and recognition of the killings as genocide are separate questions. How many people died in all. The precise sequence of the army's recovery of Har-gaysa and Boor-oh remains uncertain, because the accounts differ. The sources used here also do not establish the exact days each town fell in 1991. The sources used here do not establish the responsibility of individual S N M commanders for the documented abuses, or how many fighters the S N M had. How many died around Bo-rahma and Deela in 1991. Many suspected graves remain unexamined.
